newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Patten says Tung unable to reverse democracy.
newsitem.headline: HK's Patten says Tung unable to reverse democracy.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten said in remarks published on Thursday his post-colonial successor would not be able to reverse democratic changes made during his tenure in the territory.
"It seems to me unlikely that a change of approach or attitude is going to suddenly reverse what has been happening," Patten told the South China Morning Post in an interview.
Future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa has planned to curb civil and political liberties when he takes over from Patten after China takes Hong Kong back from Britain at midnight on June 30.

The 28th and last British colonial governor said he expected "a great deal more emphasis on continuity" by Tung, who was chosen by a China-assembled committee last December, after the sovereignty transfer.

Patten said his successors could help mould public opinion, but it would take a "brave man, or a very great man or woman, who thinks you can completely reverse social, economic, political processes which have been deep-rooted".

Patten denied that he brought an entirely new political culture to Hong Kong that allowed the development of a more open government and civil service and included democratic reforms that roused China's anger.
"I don't think I brought that into Hong Kong. I think I responded to what was already happening in Hong Kong," Patten said.
As Hong Kong became better educated and wealthier, it would have developed its own civic consciousness that would have demanded recognition had Patten not responded to it.
"I think if I had not responded to that, Hong Kong would not be as successful as it is today. There would have been a great deal of political turmoil in the last five years," he said.

"But there's an absurd argument that people in Hong Kong aren't interested in civil liberties, that somehow I introduced alien Western concepts to Hong Kong. The tens of thousands of people at Victoria Park the other night are the most eloquent response to that," he said, referring to huge crowds at Hong Kong's June 4 commemoration of the 1989 Tiananmen massacre in Beijing.

But Patten said the transition would have gone better had China not insisted on a six-month period that included the creation and operation of a provisional legislature before the transfer of sovereignty on July 1.
The China-appointed chamber will replace the current democratically elected Legislative Council on July 1.
"It would have been better if there had been no provisional legislature, or if there had to be a provisional legislature, it had not started work six months before the transition," he said.

"It would have been better if it had not started work on pieces of legislation which give the impression that the incoming government is nervous about stability in Hong Kong and about the exercise of freedoms in Hong Kong."
